t.8.1: Arjuna said: What is that Brahman, what is the adhyātma, and what is karma, O Puruṣottama? And what is declared to be the adhibhūta, and what is called the adhidaiva?
t.8.2: Who is the adhiyajña here in this body, and how does he dwell in it, O Madhusūdana? And how are you to be known at the time of departure by those whose selves are controlled?
t.8.4: The perishable state of being is the adhibhūta, and the Puruṣa is the adhidaivata; I myself, here in this body, am the adhiyajña, O best of the embodied.
t.8.3: The Blessed Lord said: The supreme imperishable is Brahman; its own essential nature is called the inner Self. The creative outpouring that brings forth the existence of beings is known as karma.
t.8.5: And whoever, at the time of death, departs while remembering Me alone, having cast off the body, attains My state of being; of this there is no doubt.
t.8.6: Whatever state of being one remembers when at the end one gives up the body, to that very state one goes, O Kaunteya, having always been absorbed in that state of being.
t.8.7: Therefore, at all times remember me and fight. With mind and intellect offered to me, you will surely come to me alone; of this there is no doubt.
t.8.8: With a mind disciplined by the yoga of constant practice and straying to nothing else, O Pārtha, one who meditates without ceasing goes to the supreme, divine Puruṣa.
t.8.9: He who meditates upon the ancient Seer, the Ruler, subtler than the subtle, the Sustainer of all, whose form is beyond thought, radiant like the sun and beyond all darkness.
t.8.10: At the time of departure, with an unmoving mind, endowed with devotion and with the strength of yoga, having made the vital breath enter fully between the brows, he reaches that supreme, divine Puruṣa.
t.8.11: That which the knowers of the Veda call the Imperishable, which ascetics free from passion enter, and desiring which they practise celibacy, that state I shall declare to you in brief.
t.8.12: Restraining all the gates of the body and confining the mind within the heart, placing his own life-breath in the head, he is established in the concentration of yoga.
t.8.13: He who has uttered Om, the one-syllabled Brahman, and departs while remembering me as he abandons the body, attains the supreme goal.
t.8.14: He who, with a mind turned to nothing else, constantly remembers me day after day, for that yogin, ever disciplined, I am easily attained, O Pārtha.
t.8.15: Having come to me, the great-souled ones, who have attained the highest perfection, do not again obtain birth, that impermanent abode of sorrow.
t.8.16: The worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are those of one who must return again, O Arjuna; but having reached me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth.
t.8.17: Those people who know day and night know that a day of Brahmā extends to a thousand yugas, and that his night likewise ends only after a thousand yugas.
t.8.18: At the coming of the day, all manifest things arise from the unmanifest; at the coming of the night, they dissolve into that very thing which is called the unmanifest.
t.8.19: This very same multitude of beings, coming into being again and again, is dissolved helplessly at the coming of night, O Pārtha, and comes forth again at the coming of day.
t.8.20: But beyond that unmanifest there is another existence, unmanifest and eternal, which does not perish when all beings perish.
t.8.21: That Unmanifest is called the Imperishable; they declare it to be the supreme goal. Having attained it, they do not return; that is my supreme abode.
t.8.22: That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, within whom all beings abide and by whom all this is pervaded, is attainable only through undivided devotion.
t.8.23: But the time at which yogins, having departed, go to non-return and also to return, that time I shall declare to you, O bull among the Bharatas.
t.8.24: Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course of the sun: departing then, people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
t.8.25: Smoke, night, and likewise the dark fortnight, the six months of the sun's southern course: there the yogī, having attained the lunar light, returns.
t.8.26: These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are indeed held to be eternal. By the one, a person goes to non-return; by the other, he returns again.
t.8.27: Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogī is ever deluded. Therefore, at all times, be steadfast in yoga, O Arjuna.
t.8.28: Whatever fruit of merit is declared for the Vedas, for sacrifices, for austerities and for gifts, the yogī who knows this goes beyond all of it and attains the supreme, primeval abode.
